examTakeaway: Buprenorphine for opioid use disorder can start without a completed inpatient detox. Detox alone is not the treatment.
scenario: A 34-year-old man uses heroin daily and wants medication treatment. He is not in respiratory failure. A colleague says he must finish a 7-day inpatient detox with no buprenorphine before any medication can be considered.
question: Does treatment have to wait for a drug-free detox week?
options: No. Buprenorphine is the treatment. A drug-free week is not required first
Yes. Seven drug-free days are mandatory before any medication
Naltrexone tonight while he is still using heroin
Methadone is illegal to discuss in any setting
Ibuprofen as the medication for opioid use disorder
correctAnswer: No. Buprenorphine is the treatment. A drug-free week is not required first
explanation:
Buprenorphine for opioid use disorder can start without a completed inpatient detox. Detox alone is not the treatment. He can be induced when withdrawal is beginning. Withholding medication for a drug-free week raises relapse risk. ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder, 2020.

No. Buprenorphine is the treatment. A drug-free week is not required first
Yes. Seven drug-free days are mandatory before any medication — Medication is the treatment. A forced drug-free week is not the gate.
Naltrexone tonight while he is still using heroin — Naltrexone would precipitate withdrawal if an opioid is still present. It is not the immediate start.
Methadone is illegal to discuss in any setting — Methadone is a treatment in licensed programs. The error is the mandatory detox delay.
Ibuprofen as the medication for opioid use disorder — An NSAID does not treat the use disorder.
citation: ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder, 2020.

examTakeaway: A healthy adult with outpatient pneumonia is treated with amoxicillin or doxycycline, not a fluoroquinolone as the first drug.
scenario: A 33-year-old woman has had cough and fever for two days. Her temperature is 38.3 C, her pulse is 96/min, and her blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg. She has no lung disease, no recent antibiotics, and no immunosuppression. A chest film shows one lobar infiltrate. A colleague prescribes levofloxacin and says every pneumonia starts with that class.
question: Which outpatient drug fits a healthy adult?
options: Levofloxacin as the preferred first drug for every outpatient
Amoxicillin or doxycycline, not levofloxacin first
No antibiotic, because the blood pressure is normal
Oseltamivir alone, with no antibacterial drug
A 21-day course of amoxicillin
correctAnswer: Amoxicillin or doxycycline, not levofloxacin first
explanation:
A healthy adult with outpatient pneumonia is treated with amoxicillin or doxycycline, not a fluoroquinolone as the first drug. She has no comorbidity and is stable enough for home. Levofloxacin is reserved for sicker or comorbid patients. ATS/IDSA 2019 guideline on community-acquired pneumonia in adults.

Amoxicillin or doxycycline, not levofloxacin first
Levofloxacin as the preferred first drug for every outpatient — Healthy outpatients are not started on a fluoroquinolone.
No antibiotic, because the blood pressure is normal — A lobar infiltrate with fever is treated.
Oseltamivir alone, with no antibacterial drug — Nothing here selects influenza as the only treatment.
A 21-day course of amoxicillin — The usual course is about 5 days when she improves, not 21 days.
citation: ATS/IDSA 2019 guideline on community-acquired pneumonia in adults.

examTakeaway: Outpatient pneumonia plus chronic heart or lung disease uses combination therapy or a respiratory fluoroquinolone, not amoxicillin alone.
scenario: A 70-year-old man with COPD has fever and a lobar infiltrate. His blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg, his pulse is 100/min, and he can take pills. A colleague prescribes amoxicillin alone, using the regimen for a healthy young adult.
question: Why is amoxicillin alone the wrong regimen?
options: Amoxicillin alone is correct at every age and every comorbidity
Immediate intubation because he is 70
COPD is a comorbidity, so he needs broader coverage than amoxicillin alone
A steroid only, and no antibiotic
Nitrofurantoin, because it treats lung infection
correctAnswer: COPD is a comorbidity, so he needs broader coverage than amoxicillin alone
explanation:
Outpatient pneumonia plus chronic heart or lung disease uses combination therapy or a respiratory fluoroquinolone, not amoxicillin alone. His COPD changes the regimen. He can still be treated by mouth because he is stable. ATS/IDSA 2019 guideline on community-acquired pneumonia in adults.

COPD is a comorbidity, so he needs broader coverage than amoxicillin alone
Amoxicillin alone is correct at every age and every comorbidity — Comorbidity is what changes the regimen.
Immediate intubation because he is 70 — Age 70 with a normal pressure and the ability to swallow is not an intubation indication.
A steroid only, and no antibiotic — The infiltrate is treated with an antibiotic. A steroid does not replace it.
Nitrofurantoin, because it treats lung infection — Nitrofurantoin does not treat pneumonia.
citation: ATS/IDSA 2019 guideline on community-acquired pneumonia in adults.

examTakeaway: Uncomplicated acute bronchitis in a healthy adult does not get an antibiotic.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman has had a cough for 8 days. Her temperature is 37.2 C, her lungs are clear, and a chest film is not indicated. She has no COPD and no immunosuppression. A colleague prescribes azithromycin because a cough that lasts a week is bacterial.
question: Does this cough need an antibiotic?
options: Yes. Every cough longer than 5 days is bacterial
Yes, but only with a fluoroquinolone
No antibiotic is ever used for any cough, including pneumonia
No. Uncomplicated bronchitis is not treated with azithromycin
A 14-day steroid burst as required therapy
correctAnswer: No. Uncomplicated bronchitis is not treated with azithromycin
explanation:
Uncomplicated acute bronchitis in a healthy adult does not get an antibiotic. Eight days of cough with a clear examination is the usual viral course. An antibiotic does not shorten it in a useful way and adds harm. CDC antibiotic prescribing guidance, 2024: uncomplicated acute bronchitis in otherwise healthy adults does not get antibiotics.

No. Uncomplicated bronchitis is not treated with azithromycin
Yes. Every cough longer than 5 days is bacterial — Duration alone does not make bronchitis bacterial.
Yes, but only with a fluoroquinolone — A fluoroquinolone is also an antibiotic she does not need.
No antibiotic is ever used for any cough, including pneumonia — Pneumonia is treated. She does not have it.
A 14-day steroid burst as required therapy — A long steroid course is not the treatment of uncomplicated bronchitis.
citation: CDC antibiotic prescribing guidance, 2024: uncomplicated acute bronchitis in otherwise healthy adults does not get antibiotics.

examTakeaway: A long-acting beta agonist is never used as the only asthma drug. It has to be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid.
scenario: A 31-year-old man with asthma is prescribed salmeterol alone. He uses it daily and has no inhaled corticosteroid. He wheezes most days. A colleague says the long-acting drug replaces the need for an anti-inflammatory inhaler.
question: Why is salmeterol alone unsafe?
options: Salmeterol alone is the preferred controller
Stop every inhaler because wheeze most days is too mild to treat
Oral theophylline as a safe substitute for the corticosteroid
Add a second long-acting beta agonist and still skip the corticosteroid
A long-acting beta agonist without an inhaled corticosteroid increases severe attacks
correctAnswer: A long-acting beta agonist without an inhaled corticosteroid increases severe attacks
explanation:
A long-acting beta agonist is never used as the only asthma drug. It has to be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid. Daily wheeze needs an anti-inflammatory drug. Salmeterol alone is the regimen the reports tell clinicians not to use. Global Initiative for Asthma, GINA Strategy Report 2025.

A long-acting beta agonist without an inhaled corticosteroid increases severe attacks
Salmeterol alone is the preferred controller — It is not. The anti-inflammatory drug is required.
Stop every inhaler because wheeze most days is too mild to treat — Symptoms most days are a reason to treat, not to stop.
Oral theophylline as a safe substitute for the corticosteroid — A methylxanthine does not replace the inhaled corticosteroid.
Add a second long-acting beta agonist and still skip the corticosteroid — A second bronchodilator still leaves inflammation untreated.
citation: Global Initiative for Asthma, GINA Strategy Report 2025.

examTakeaway: Nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with a high stroke score is anticoagulated with a DOAC. Aspirin alone is not the stroke drug.
scenario: A 76-year-old man has atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 4. He has no mechanical valve and no mitral stenosis. His creatinine clearance is 70 mL/min. A colleague starts aspirin 81 mg and says anticoagulation is only for a score above 6.
question: Which stroke prevention fits a score of 4?
options: A direct oral anticoagulant, not aspirin alone
Aspirin 81 mg as sufficient stroke prevention
No drug until the score reaches 6
Dual antiplatelet therapy instead of anticoagulation
A DOAC only if a mechanical valve is also present
correctAnswer: A direct oral anticoagulant, not aspirin alone
explanation:
Nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with a high stroke score is anticoagulated with a DOAC. Aspirin alone is not the stroke drug. A score of 4 in a man is well above the treatment line. He can take a DOAC. Warfarin is not required because he has no valve disease that forces it. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation.

A direct oral anticoagulant, not aspirin alone
Aspirin 81 mg as sufficient stroke prevention — Aspirin does not replace anticoagulation at this score.
No drug until the score reaches 6 — Treatment is indicated well below 6.
Dual antiplatelet therapy instead of anticoagulation — Two antiplatelet drugs are not the stroke regimen for this score.
A DOAC only if a mechanical valve is also present — A mechanical valve would push him to warfarin, not be required before a DOAC.
citation: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation.

examTakeaway: A mechanical mitral valve is anticoagulated with warfarin. A DOAC is not a substitute.
scenario: A 62-year-old woman has a mechanical mitral valve and atrial fibrillation. Her INR has been hard to check, so a colleague switches her from warfarin to apixaban and says all atrial fibrillation now uses a DOAC.
question: Why is apixaban the wrong switch?
options: Apixaban is preferred for every mechanical valve
The mechanical mitral valve requires warfarin. Atrial fibrillation does not override that
Stop anticoagulation because the valve is mechanical and therefore protected
Aspirin alone replaces warfarin after the first year
A DOAC is acceptable if the INR has ever been therapeutic
correctAnswer: The mechanical mitral valve requires warfarin. Atrial fibrillation does not override that
explanation:
A mechanical mitral valve is anticoagulated with warfarin. A DOAC is not a substitute. The atrial fibrillation would have allowed a DOAC only if the valve were not mechanical. The valve is the fact that keeps warfarin. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease.

The mechanical mitral valve requires warfarin. Atrial fibrillation does not override that
Apixaban is preferred for every mechanical valve — Mechanical valves stay on warfarin.
Stop anticoagulation because the valve is mechanical and therefore protected — The mechanical valve is the reason anticoagulation continues.
Aspirin alone replaces warfarin after the first year — Aspirin does not replace warfarin for this valve.
A DOAC is acceptable if the INR has ever been therapeutic — A past therapeutic INR does not create a DOAC indication.
citation: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease.

examTakeaway: Moderate or severe mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation is anticoagulated with warfarin, not a DOAC.
scenario: A 58-year-old man has atrial fibrillation and moderate mitral stenosis from rheumatic disease. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3. A colleague starts rivaroxaban because the score, not the valve, chooses the drug.
question: Which anticoagulant fits the stenosis?
options: Rivaroxaban, because a score of 3 always selects a DOAC
Aspirin, because stenosis lowers stroke risk
Warfarin. The stenosis excludes a DOAC
No anticoagulant if the stenosis is only moderate
Dual antiplatelet therapy for one month and then nothing
correctAnswer: Warfarin. The stenosis excludes a DOAC
explanation:
Moderate or severe mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation is anticoagulated with warfarin, not a DOAC. The score shows he needs anticoagulation. It does not show that a DOAC is allowed. Rheumatic stenosis is the exclusion. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation.

Warfarin. The stenosis excludes a DOAC
Rivaroxaban, because a score of 3 always selects a DOAC — The score selects anticoagulation. The stenosis selects warfarin.
Aspirin, because stenosis lowers stroke risk — Stenosis does not lower the need for anticoagulation.
No anticoagulant if the stenosis is only moderate — Moderate stenosis is already the exclusion for a DOAC and still needs anticoagulation.
Dual antiplatelet therapy for one month and then nothing — A month of antiplatelet drugs does not treat this valve lesion.
citation: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation.

examTakeaway: A nitrate and a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor together can cause severe hypotension. The combination is contraindicated.
scenario: A 64-year-old man takes sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. He now has angina and a blood pressure of 136/80 mm Hg. A colleague gives sublingual nitroglycerin and says the sildenafil he took four hours ago is irrelevant.
question: Why is the nitroglycerin unsafe right now?
options: The nitrate is required, and sildenafil does not interact with it
Give the nitrate only if the pressure is already below 100
Double the sildenafil so the angina stops
He took sildenafil four hours ago, and a nitrate is contraindicated with that drug
The interaction lasts only 30 minutes, so four hours is safe
correctAnswer: He took sildenafil four hours ago, and a nitrate is contraindicated with that drug
explanation:
A nitrate and a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor together can cause severe hypotension. The combination is contraindicated. Four hours is well inside the interaction window. A pressure of 136 does not make the combination safe. FDA prescribing information for nitroglycerin, 2023 label: nitrates are contraindicated with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.

He took sildenafil four hours ago, and a nitrate is contraindicated with that drug
The nitrate is required, and sildenafil does not interact with it — The interaction is a labeled contraindication.
Give the nitrate only if the pressure is already below 100 — A low pressure would be another reason to avoid a nitrate, not the condition that makes this pair safe.
Double the sildenafil so the angina stops — More of the erectile drug does not treat angina and deepens the interaction.
The interaction lasts only 30 minutes, so four hours is safe — The window is many hours, not 30 minutes.
citation: FDA prescribing information for nitroglycerin, 2023 label: nitrates are contraindicated with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.

examTakeaway: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is referred for valve replacement. Medical therapy does not replace the valve.
scenario: A 78-year-old woman has exertional syncope. The valve area is 0.8 cm2 and the mean gradient is 48 mm Hg. Her ejection fraction is 60 percent. A colleague starts a beta blocker and says surgery can wait until she has chest pain as well as syncope.
question: What does syncope plus this valve area mean?
options: A beta blocker is definitive therapy, so no referral is needed
Referral only after a second syncope
Balloon the valve and never replace it, because the ejection fraction is 60 percent
Start a nitrate for the syncope
Refer for valve replacement. Syncope is already a severe symptom
correctAnswer: Refer for valve replacement. Syncope is already a severe symptom
explanation:
Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is referred for valve replacement. Medical therapy does not replace the valve. A valve area of 0.8 cm2 and a gradient of 48 mm Hg are severe, and syncope is a classic symptom. Waiting for chest pain adds a risk the guideline does not ask for. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease.

Refer for valve replacement. Syncope is already a severe symptom
A beta blocker is definitive therapy, so no referral is needed — No pill replaces the valve once symptoms and severe stenosis are both present.
Referral only after a second syncope — The first syncope is enough.
Balloon the valve and never replace it, because the ejection fraction is 60 percent — A preserved ejection fraction does not cancel replacement. Balloon valvuloplasty is not the destination therapy.
Start a nitrate for the syncope — A nitrate can drop preload in severe stenosis. It is not the treatment.
citation: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease.

examTakeaway: Hypothyroidism in pregnancy is treated by increasing levothyroxine. Methimazole is not a treatment for a high TSH.
scenario: A 30-year-old woman is at 8 weeks and takes levothyroxine 75 mcg. TSH is 6.2 mIU/L and free T4 is low-normal. She feels cold. A colleague stops levothyroxine and starts methimazole because a thyroid number in pregnancy is treated with an antithyroid drug.
question: Which direction does the levothyroxine dose move?
options: Increase it. Methimazole treats an overactive gland, which she does not have
Stop levothyroxine and start methimazole
No change until after delivery
Radioiodine this month
Iodine drops in place of the hormone
correctAnswer: Increase it. Methimazole treats an overactive gland, which she does not have
explanation:
Hypothyroidism in pregnancy is treated by increasing levothyroxine. Methimazole is not a treatment for a high TSH. A TSH of 6.2 in the first trimester is above the pregnancy target. Stopping the hormone would worsen the deficit. 2017 American Thyroid Association guidelines on thyroid disease in pregnancy.

Increase it. Methimazole treats an overactive gland, which she does not have
Stop levothyroxine and start methimazole — Methimazole is for hyperthyroidism. Her TSH is high, not suppressed.
No change until after delivery — The dose is adjusted during pregnancy, not deferred until birth.
Radioiodine this month — Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Iodine drops in place of the hormone — Iodine does not replace levothyroxine when the TSH is already high on treatment.
citation: 2017 American Thyroid Association guidelines on thyroid disease in pregnancy.

examTakeaway: In the first trimester, propylthiouracil is preferred over methimazole for hyperthyroidism because methimazole is more teratogenic then.
scenario: A 27-year-old woman is at 9 weeks with a TSH below 0.01 mIU/L, a high free T4, and tremor. She is not in storm. A colleague starts methimazole and says the trimester does not change the drug.
question: Which antithyroid drug fits 9 weeks?
options: Methimazole, because the trimester never changes the choice
Propylthiouracil during the first trimester, not methimazole
Radioiodine at 9 weeks
Levothyroxine, because tremor means the gland is underactive
No drug until the second trimester
correctAnswer: Propylthiouracil during the first trimester, not methimazole
explanation:
In the first trimester, propylthiouracil is preferred over methimazole for hyperthyroidism because methimazole is more teratogenic then. Nine weeks is the first trimester. After that window the drugs may be reconsidered because propylthiouracil has liver toxicity. Right now the trimester chooses the drug. 2017 American Thyroid Association guidelines on thyroid disease in pregnancy.

Propylthiouracil during the first trimester, not methimazole
Methimazole, because the trimester never changes the choice — The first trimester is exactly when the choice changes.
Radioiodine at 9 weeks — Radioiodine is not used in pregnancy.
Levothyroxine, because tremor means the gland is underactive — A suppressed TSH and a high free T4 are overactivity.
No drug until the second trimester — Overt hyperthyroidism is treated now. The drug is what changes, not the decision to treat.
citation: 2017 American Thyroid Association guidelines on thyroid disease in pregnancy.

examTakeaway: If potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L in diabetic ketoacidosis, potassium is replaced before insulin. Insulin would drive the potassium lower.
scenario: A 19-year-old man has glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and potassium 2.9 mEq/L. He is breathing deeply. A colleague starts intravenous insulin immediately and says the potassium can be replaced later.
question: What happens to insulin while potassium is 2.9 mEq/L?
options: Start insulin now and replace potassium only if it falls under 2.0
Bicarbonate first and no potassium
Hold insulin and replace potassium first
Insulin is contraindicated for the entire admission once potassium has been low
Oral potassium only, with no intravenous plan, because he is awake
correctAnswer: Hold insulin and replace potassium first
explanation:
If potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L in diabetic ketoacidosis, potassium is replaced before insulin. Insulin would drive the potassium lower. The pH shows he needs insulin soon, but not while the potassium is 2.9. ADA consensus report on hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes, 2024.

Hold insulin and replace potassium first
Start insulin now and replace potassium only if it falls under 2.0 — The hold threshold is 3.3, not 2.0.
Bicarbonate first and no potassium — Bicarbonate is not the priority at this potassium.
Insulin is contraindicated for the entire admission once potassium has been low — The hold is until potassium is repleted, not a permanent ban.
Oral potassium only, with no intravenous plan, because he is awake — Severe deficit in ketoacidosis is replaced promptly, and insulin waits.
citation: ADA consensus report on hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes, 2024.

examTakeaway: Migraine with aura makes combined hormonal contraception an unacceptable risk. A progestin-only method does not carry that same estrogen risk.
scenario: A 26-year-old woman has migraine with visual aura. She wants contraception and has no hypertension. A colleague prescribes a combined estrogen-progestin pill and says aura does not change eligibility.
question: Why is the combined pill the wrong method?
options: Combined pills are preferred when aura is present
No contraceptive method is safe once aura exists
The risk applies only after age 45
Aura puts combined hormonal contraception in the unacceptable-risk category
Add an estrogen patch on top of the pill
correctAnswer: Aura puts combined hormonal contraception in the unacceptable-risk category
explanation:
Migraine with aura makes combined hormonal contraception an unacceptable risk. A progestin-only method does not carry that same estrogen risk. The concern is stroke. A normal blood pressure does not remove the aura. CDC U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2024.

Aura puts combined hormonal contraception in the unacceptable-risk category
Combined pills are preferred when aura is present — Aura is a reason to avoid estrogen, not to prefer it.
No contraceptive method is safe once aura exists — Progestin-only methods and intrauterine devices remain options.
The risk applies only after age 45 — Age 26 with aura is already unacceptable for combined hormones.
Add an estrogen patch on top of the pill — More estrogen deepens the problem.
citation: CDC U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2024.

examTakeaway: Long-term metformin is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. Numbness or anemia is a reason to check B12, not to ignore it because glucose is controlled.
scenario: A 64-year-old man has taken metformin for 8 years. A1c is 6.9 percent. He has numb feet and a hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL with a high mean cell volume. A colleague says the numbness is expected aging and does not check B12.
question: Which level should be checked?
options: No level. Numbness on metformin is normal and untested
A folate level only, because metformin depletes folate and not B12
Stop checking forever if one glucose is normal
An immediate switch to a sulfonylurea without a B12 level
Vitamin B12, because long-term metformin and this blood count point to deficiency
correctAnswer: Vitamin B12, because long-term metformin and this blood count point to deficiency
explanation:
Long-term metformin is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. Numbness or anemia is a reason to check B12, not to ignore it because glucose is controlled. A high mean cell volume with numbness is the pattern. A controlled A1c does not answer it. American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes, 2026.

Vitamin B12, because long-term metformin and this blood count point to deficiency
No level. Numbness on metformin is normal and untested — The standards specifically tie this drug to B12 deficiency.
A folate level only, because metformin depletes folate and not B12 — The deficiency linked to metformin is B12.
Stop checking forever if one glucose is normal — Glucose control is not a B12 result.
An immediate switch to a sulfonylurea without a B12 level — The level explains the numbness. A sulfonylurea does not diagnose it.
citation: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes, 2026.

examTakeaway: Strongly anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin are avoided in older adults because of confusion, constipation, and falls.
scenario: An 82-year-old woman has urge incontinence. She already has mild forgetfulness. A colleague starts oxybutynin and says bladder drugs do not affect thinking.
question: Why is oxybutynin a poor choice at age 82?
options: It is a strong anticholinergic drug, which the Beers Criteria say to avoid in older adults
Oxybutynin is preferred after age 80 because confusion protects the bladder
The age cutoff for this warning is 95
Double the dose if she becomes more confused
Add diphenhydramine at night so the bladder drug works better
correctAnswer: It is a strong anticholinergic drug, which the Beers Criteria say to avoid in older adults
explanation:
Strongly anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin are avoided in older adults because of confusion, constipation, and falls. She already has forgetfulness. A non-drug bladder strategy or a less anticholinergic option is preferred. American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria, 2023.

It is a strong anticholinergic drug, which the Beers Criteria say to avoid in older adults
Oxybutynin is preferred after age 80 because confusion protects the bladder — Confusion is a harm, not a benefit.
The age cutoff for this warning is 95 — The criteria apply to older adults, and 82 is inside that group.
Double the dose if she becomes more confused — More drug would worsen the anticholinergic effect.
Add diphenhydramine at night so the bladder drug works better — Diphenhydramine is another strong anticholinergic drug and adds the same harm.
citation: American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria, 2023.

examTakeaway: When immune thrombocytopenia needs a rapid platelet rise for surgery or serious bleeding, IVIG or a similar rescue is used. Steroids alone are too slow for that emergency.
scenario: A 45-year-old man with immune thrombocytopenia has a platelet count of 8,000. He needs urgent surgery for a perforated ulcer tonight. A colleague starts prednisone and says the count will be high enough by morning without IVIG.
question: What raises the count fast enough for tonight?
options: Prednisone alone, because every count responds by the next morning
IVIG, because a corticosteroid will not lift the count in time for surgery tonight
Aspirin so the remaining platelets are stickier
No drug, because surgery can proceed at 8,000
Heparin to prevent a clot from the low count
correctAnswer: IVIG, because a corticosteroid will not lift the count in time for surgery tonight
explanation:
When immune thrombocytopenia needs a rapid platelet rise for surgery or serious bleeding, IVIG or a similar rescue is used. Steroids alone are too slow for that emergency. Prednisone can still be part of care. It is not the drug that fixes tonight. ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

IVIG, because a corticosteroid will not lift the count in time for surgery tonight
Prednisone alone, because every count responds by the next morning — Steroids take longer than one night.
Aspirin so the remaining platelets are stickier — Aspirin is contraindicated at this count.
No drug, because surgery can proceed at 8,000 — A perforated ulcer cannot wait on a count of 8,000 without an attempt to raise it.
Heparin to prevent a clot from the low count — Heparin does not treat immune thrombocytopenia.
citation: ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

examTakeaway: Platelet transfusion is not given for the low count of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia unless there is serious bleeding.
scenario: A 70-year-old woman has a high 4T score and platelets of 55,000. She has no bleeding. A colleague transfuses platelets to 100,000 before starting a non-heparin anticoagulant.
question: Is the transfusion needed before the anticoagulant?
options: Yes. The anticoagulant cannot start until the count is 100,000
Yes, and heparin is continued during the transfusion
No. Transfusion is for serious bleeding, which she does not have
Transfuse only if the count is above 150,000
No anticoagulant and no transfusion, because a count of 55,000 cannot clot
correctAnswer: No. Transfusion is for serious bleeding, which she does not have
explanation:
Platelet transfusion is not given for the low count of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia unless there is serious bleeding. She needs the heparin stopped and a non-heparin anticoagulant. Raising the count with a transfusion is not a prerequisite and can add thrombosis. ASH 2018 guidelines for management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

No. Transfusion is for serious bleeding, which she does not have
Yes. The anticoagulant cannot start until the count is 100,000 — The anticoagulant starts because of the thrombosis risk. The count is not first transfused to 100,000.
Yes, and heparin is continued during the transfusion — Heparin stops. Transfusion does not make heparin safe.
Transfuse only if the count is above 150,000 — That is not a transfusion trigger in either direction.
No anticoagulant and no transfusion, because a count of 55,000 cannot clot — The disease causes thrombosis despite the low count.
citation: ASH 2018 guidelines for management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

examTakeaway: Iron deficiency anemia in a postmenopausal woman is evaluated with bidirectional endoscopy, not iron tablets alone.
scenario: A 68-year-old woman has hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, ferritin 8 ng/mL, and no visible blood. She is postmenopausal. A colleague starts oral iron and says endoscopy is only for male patients.
question: What evaluation accompanies the iron?
options: Iron tablets and no procedure, because only male patients are endoscoped
A bone-marrow biopsy before any endoscopy
Oral iron for a year, then a scan if the hemoglobin is still low
Bidirectional endoscopy, because postmenopausal iron deficiency is a gastrointestinal source until proved otherwise
Stool culture as the only test
correctAnswer: Bidirectional endoscopy, because postmenopausal iron deficiency is a gastrointestinal source until proved otherwise
explanation:
Iron deficiency anemia in a postmenopausal woman is evaluated with bidirectional endoscopy, not iron tablets alone. Ferritin of 8 confirms iron deficiency. Sex does not remove the need to look for a colon or gastric source. AGA clinical practice guidelines on the gastrointestinal evaluation of iron deficiency anemia, 2020.

Bidirectional endoscopy, because postmenopausal iron deficiency is a gastrointestinal source until proved otherwise
Iron tablets and no procedure, because only male patients are endoscoped — Postmenopausal patients are evaluated the same way.
A bone-marrow biopsy before any endoscopy — Marrow is not the first study when ferritin is 8.
Oral iron for a year, then a scan if the hemoglobin is still low — A year of uninvestigated deficiency misses a lesion.
Stool culture as the only test — Culture does not find the usual bleeding source.
citation: AGA clinical practice guidelines on the gastrointestinal evaluation of iron deficiency anemia, 2020.

examTakeaway: Cancer-associated venous thrombosis is treated with a DOAC or low-molecular-weight heparin, not warfarin as the automatic first drug.
scenario: A 63-year-old man with metastatic colon cancer has a new femoral-vein thrombus. He is not bleeding and his creatinine clearance is 80 mL/min. A colleague starts warfarin alone and says cancer patients cannot use a DOAC or heparin.
question: Which anticoagulant class is appropriate?
options: Warfarin alone as the required first drug
Aspirin 325 mg as sufficient treatment of a femoral thrombus
No anticoagulant because cancer is a bleeding disease only
Inferior vena cava filter as the first treatment in every cancer thrombus
A DOAC or low-molecular-weight heparin, not warfarin as the default
correctAnswer: A DOAC or low-molecular-weight heparin, not warfarin as the default
explanation:
Cancer-associated venous thrombosis is treated with a DOAC or low-molecular-weight heparin, not warfarin as the automatic first drug. He is not bleeding and his kidneys can clear a DOAC. Warfarin is not forbidden forever, but it is not the automatic first choice. ASCO guideline update on venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and treatment in patients with cancer, 2023.

A DOAC or low-molecular-weight heparin, not warfarin as the default
Warfarin alone as the required first drug — The update moved away from warfarin as the default.
Aspirin 325 mg as sufficient treatment of a femoral thrombus — Aspirin does not treat an acute deep-vein thrombus.
No anticoagulant because cancer is a bleeding disease only — Cancer is also a clotting disease. The thrombus is treated.
Inferior vena cava filter as the first treatment in every cancer thrombus — A filter is not first-line when anticoagulation can be used.
citation: ASCO guideline update on venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and treatment in patients with cancer, 2023.

examTakeaway: Moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnea is treated with positive airway pressure, not with a sedative as the sleep drug.
scenario: A 56-year-old man stops breathing during sleep. A study shows an apnea-hypopnea index of 32 events per hour. He is sleepy while driving. A colleague prescribes a nightly benzodiazepine and says a pressure device is optional cosmetics.
question: Which treatment matches an index of 32?
options: Positive airway pressure, not a nightly benzodiazepine
A benzodiazepine as the primary treatment
No treatment until the index exceeds 100
Antibiotics for the pauses
Oxygen by nasal cannula alone as an equal substitute
correctAnswer: Positive airway pressure, not a nightly benzodiazepine
explanation:
Moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnea is treated with positive airway pressure, not with a sedative as the sleep drug. An index of 32 is severe. A benzodiazepine can worsen the pauses. American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline on positive airway pressure for obstructive sleep apnea, 2019.

Positive airway pressure, not a nightly benzodiazepine
A benzodiazepine as the primary treatment — A sedative can deepen the obstruction.
No treatment until the index exceeds 100 — Severe disease begins well below 100. Thirty-two is already severe.
Antibiotics for the pauses — The pauses are not an infection.
Oxygen by nasal cannula alone as an equal substitute — Oxygen does not stent the airway the way positive pressure does.
citation: American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline on positive airway pressure for obstructive sleep apnea, 2019.

examTakeaway: Suspected adrenal crisis is treated immediately with intravenous hydrocortisone and saline. A lab result is not required before the first dose.
scenario: A 46-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency has vomiting and a blood pressure of 78/50 mm Hg after a flu-like illness. She missed her tablets. Glucose is 58 mg/dL. A colleague waits for a cortisol result before any steroid.
question: What is given while the cortisol is pending?
options: No steroid until the cortisol result returns
Intravenous hydrocortisone and saline now
Oral prednisone tablets, which she is currently vomiting
Insulin, because the glucose is 58 mg/dL
Antibiotics only, with no steroid
correctAnswer: Intravenous hydrocortisone and saline now
explanation:
Suspected adrenal crisis is treated immediately with intravenous hydrocortisone and saline. A lab result is not required before the first dose. She is hypotensive, hypoglycemic, and has missed her replacement. Waiting for a number delays the drug that treats the crisis. Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on primary adrenal insufficiency, 2016.

Intravenous hydrocortisone and saline now
No steroid until the cortisol result returns — The crisis is treated on suspicion.
Oral prednisone tablets, which she is currently vomiting — She is vomiting. The route is intravenous.
Insulin, because the glucose is 58 mg/dL — A glucose of 58 is low. Insulin would make it lower.
Antibiotics only, with no steroid — Infection may have triggered the crisis. It does not replace the steroid.
citation: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on primary adrenal insufficiency, 2016.

examTakeaway: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated. The same culture in a nonpregnant adult is not.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman is at 14 weeks. She has no urinary burning. A screening culture grows more than 100,000 colonies of E. coli. A colleague does not treat it, using the rule written for nonpregnant adults.
question: Does pregnancy change that rule?
options: No. Pregnancy uses the same do-not-treat rule
Treat only after a fever starts
Yes. Treat the bacteriuria. The do-not-treat rule is for nonpregnant adults
Nitrofurantoin is banned for the entire pregnancy, so no drug exists
A 6-week fluoroquinolone course
correctAnswer: Yes. Treat the bacteriuria. The do-not-treat rule is for nonpregnant adults
explanation:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated. The same culture in a nonpregnant adult is not. She is at 14 weeks, which is why the culture was obtained. Leaving it untreated raises the risk of a kidney infection. US Preventive Services Task Force asymptomatic bacteriuria recommendation, 2019: screen and treat pregnant persons.

Yes. Treat the bacteriuria. The do-not-treat rule is for nonpregnant adults
No. Pregnancy uses the same do-not-treat rule — Pregnancy is the exception that is treated.
Treat only after a fever starts — The point of screening is to treat before a kidney infection.
Nitrofurantoin is banned for the entire pregnancy, so no drug exists — Safe options exist. The decision is to treat, with a drug appropriate for the trimester.
A 6-week fluoroquinolone course — A long fluoroquinolone course is not the pregnancy regimen.
citation: US Preventive Services Task Force asymptomatic bacteriuria recommendation, 2019: screen and treat pregnant persons.

examTakeaway: When phosphate is high and calcium is already high, a non-calcium binder such as sevelamer is used. More calcium binder would worsen the calcium.
scenario: A 70-year-old man on dialysis has a phosphate of 7.2 mg/dL. He also has a calcium of 10.8 mg/dL. A colleague increases calcium acetate and says every phosphate binder should contain calcium.
question: Which binder fits a calcium of 10.8 mg/dL?
options: More calcium acetate, because every binder should contain calcium
No binder until phosphate exceeds 12
A thiazide to lower phosphate
A non-calcium binder such as sevelamer, not more calcium acetate
Stop dialysis because the phosphate is a lab error
correctAnswer: A non-calcium binder such as sevelamer, not more calcium acetate
explanation:
When phosphate is high and calcium is already high, a non-calcium binder such as sevelamer is used. More calcium binder would worsen the calcium. The phosphate of 7.2 still needs binding. The calcium chooses which binder. KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guideline update.

A non-calcium binder such as sevelamer, not more calcium acetate
More calcium acetate, because every binder should contain calcium — High calcium is the reason to avoid a calcium binder.
No binder until phosphate exceeds 12 — A phosphate of 7.2 is already high enough to treat.
A thiazide to lower phosphate — A thiazide is not a phosphate binder.
Stop dialysis because the phosphate is a lab error — The number is a reason to change the binder, not to stop dialysis.
citation: KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guideline update.

examTakeaway: An acute multiple-sclerosis relapse that limits function is treated with high-dose corticosteroid. A disease-modifying injection is not the acute relapse drug.
scenario: A 29-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis cannot walk her usual distance because of a new dense leg weakness for two days. She has no fever. A colleague increases her disease-modifying injection and says steroids are only for the first diagnostic relapse.
question: What treats this new weakness?
options: Only an increase in the disease-modifying injection
Antibiotics for presumed spinal infection
No treatment because a relapse must last 30 days
Aspirin as the relapse drug
High-dose corticosteroid now, not a bigger disease-modifying dose as the acute treatment
correctAnswer: High-dose corticosteroid now, not a bigger disease-modifying dose as the acute treatment
explanation:
An acute multiple-sclerosis relapse that limits function is treated with high-dose corticosteroid. A disease-modifying injection is not the acute relapse drug. Two days of dense weakness is a relapse. The disease-modifying drug stays for prevention. It does not replace the steroid. AAN 2018 practice guideline: an acute multiple-sclerosis relapse that causes disability is treated with high-dose corticosteroid.

High-dose corticosteroid now, not a bigger disease-modifying dose as the acute treatment
Only an increase in the disease-modifying injection — That drug does not treat the acute relapse.
Antibiotics for presumed spinal infection — She has no fever, and the history is a relapse pattern.
No treatment because a relapse must last 30 days — Two days of disabling weakness is treated.
Aspirin as the relapse drug — Aspirin is not the relapse treatment.
citation: AAN 2018 practice guideline: an acute multiple-sclerosis relapse that causes disability is treated with high-dose corticosteroid.
